posts.title: Plango watches AI agents on your Mac
posts.promise: Review agent activity, connections and access from one Mac security app.
posts.whatItIs: Plango describes a Mac security app for developers using coding agents. Its page says it can watch agent actions, show MCP server connections, scan skills and plugins, and let people set rules for events and requests.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers who want visibility into local AI agent activity might pay for this kind of Mac security tool. The page lists a subscription, but does not establish customer demand.
loop: Install the app on a compatible Apple silicon Mac running macOS 15 or newer.
Connect or use a coding agent supported by the product.
Review the events, requests, decisions and blocks Plango displays.
Set rules for agent access or connections that you want to control.
Check blocked actions and adjust rules yourself when needed.
posts.evidence: The attached product page describes agent monitoring, MCP visibility, skill and plugin checks, access controls, and an event view with configurable rules. It lists a seven-day trial and a $4.99 monthly subscription, and specifies compatible Mac requirements.
posts.uncertainty: This is the product maker's own description, not independent evidence of security effectiveness or customer use. People still need to judge alerts, set appropriate rules, and decide whether to allow actions; the page does not establish that every risk is detected.
first24Hours: Check whether your Mac meets the stated Apple silicon, macOS and memory requirements.
Read the product's terms and privacy information before creating an account.
If you try it, review the event view and note which decisions still need your judgment.

ease.reason: The page gives a trial and signup path, but the experiment requires a compatible Apple silicon Mac and agent setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: developers concerned about agent access could be buyers; the listed subscription does not show demand or sales.

feasibility.reason: A four-week review of the app's event view is plausible, though compatibility and actual security performance need checking.

autonomy.reason: The page describes ongoing monitoring and rule-based blocks, while people must configure rules and assess alerts.

evidence.reason: The first-party page describes product features and trial access, but supplies no independent working demonstration or real-use evidence.

posts.title: Kucedr turns a creative brief into a poster draft
posts.promise: Explore image directions, choose one and save a handoff brief with an AI desktop assistant.
posts.whatItIs: Kucedr is presented as a desktop AI assistant for writing, research, coding and media creation. Its attached page shows an exhibition-poster example: generate a concept, compare alternatives, draft a caption and layout, then save a brief for a designer.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: an individual creator or small team might pay for a desktop assistant that helps prepare creative drafts. The attached page does not establish paying customers.
loop: Describe a creative task and provide the relevant files or context.
Ask for an initial image or draft, then inspect the result.
Request alternatives and choose a direction yourself.
Ask for supporting copy or layout suggestions.
Save a brief and fill in missing details before handing it to a person.
posts.evidence: The attached Kucedr page demonstrates an exhibition poster concept, three directions for comparison, a caption and layout suggestion, and a saved brief. It describes desktop availability for macOS, Linux and Windows and lists scheduled tasks that run while Kucedr remains open.
posts.uncertainty: The page's example is a product demonstration, not evidence of customer outcomes. Generated artwork and text need human review; the demonstrated brief still lacked the date and venue. Scheduled work depends on configuration and keeping the app open.
first24Hours: Choose a small creative brief with no sensitive material.
Download Kucedr for your operating system and connect a provider if you decide to try it.
Generate one draft, review it, and record what details a human must correct.

ease.reason: The page gives a download path and a concrete poster workflow, but use requires a model/provider choice and task setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: creators or small teams might pay for drafting help, but the attached page provides no buyer or revenue evidence.

feasibility.reason: A beginner can try the shown poster-to-brief workflow in four weeks using the listed desktop downloads and a bounded creative task.

autonomy.reason: The example automates generation and brief saving, but a person chooses among directions and supplies missing details; schedules require Kucedr open.

evidence.reason: The first-party page includes a specific poster workflow and outputs, but no independent evidence of real customer use.

posts.title: Gsearch gives agents Google result data
posts.promise: A self-hosted search tool returns result links and related Google page content to an AI agent.
posts.whatItIs: Gsearch is a public repository for an MCP server, a way for an AI tool to call another tool. Its README says it uses a Firefox-based browser to retrieve Google results and returns typed JSON, including resolved result URLs and, when present, AI Overview and related questions.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers who want Google results in an agent workflow might pay for support or related services, but the repository describes the tool as self-hosted and no API key required; it gives no buyer evidence.
loop: Read the repository's legal and responsible-use guidance before trying live searches.
Install the package using one of the README's listed methods and run its setup.
Connect the MCP server to a compatible agent using the generated configuration.
Ask a bounded search question and inspect the returned links and text.
Check the sources yourself and stop if access is blocked or use is not appropriate.
posts.evidence: The attached public repository README describes installation, setup, MCP client configuration and a live search example. It says results include resolved URLs and typed fields, reports a limit of up to 20 searches per hour without a proxy, and warns that automated access may breach Google's terms.
posts.uncertainty: These are repository claims and demonstration details, not independent verification of reliability. The README explicitly places terms-of-service risk on the user. A human must review source quality, legal and policy constraints, and any search results before relying on them.
first24Hours: Read the repository's legal and responsible-use guidance and decide whether a test is appropriate.
Review the setup instructions and requirements before installing anything.
If you proceed, try one low-stakes query and manually verify each result from its destination page.

ease.reason: The README provides setup instructions, but installation includes downloading a browser and configuring an MCP client.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: agent developers might value this workflow, but the README describes a self-hosted tool and supplies no buyer evidence.

feasibility.reason: A small four-week test is technically bounded by the documented setup and one search flow, with browser setup and access constraints to resolve.

autonomy.reason: The server automates browser retrieval and structured output, but humans must check results and judge legal and access limits.

evidence.reason: The repository supplies setup instructions and a live-call demonstration, but its performance claims are maker-reported and not independently checked here.
